The Nasdaq-100 is cheaper on forward earnings today than it was at the bottom of the dot-com crash.

The 2002 number needs its context. That ~20-25x sat on earnings that had collapsed, so it was never actually cheap. Today's ~17x sits on earnings that are real and still growing. Same multiple math, opposite setup.

The tech premium has vanished too. The Nasdaq-100 now trades at roughly the same forward multiple as the S&P 500. Cheap does not mean the selling is over, the tape still has to confirm the turn. But the valuation case for the Nasdaq has not been this strong since the last time it bottomed.

The administration is preparing findings from a Section 301 probe into excess industrial capacity across 16 trading partners, with rates up to 20% on China, 15% on the EU, Japan, Korea and Taiwan, and higher still on Vietnam and India. The tariffs could begin in January after hearings, and the US-China truce expires Jan 10, so the calendar is tight. Asia's chip names sold off hard on it, and the US tape followed. The market's fear is not the tariff itself, it is the second-order effect: tariffs on industrial capacity mean higher input costs for the same companies building the AI data centers, and slower global growth while the Fed is hiking. The probe is a process with hearings, which means headlines will keep coming. The trade is not to guess the outcome, it is to know the dates: hearings, January, Jan 10.

posts.text: The bond market disagreed with the inflation print on yesterday , and the bond market is usually the one worth listening to. Core PCE came in a tenth hot, GDP was revised up to a strong number, and the 10-year yield fell anyway, down more than 9 basis points to around 4.81%. Yields fall when the market fears growth more than inflation, and that is the read. The tape sold off on tariff headlines, not on the inflation number, and the bond market said the hiking path is already priced. A December hike is the base case and everyone knows it. What the bond market is pricing now is what comes after: a Fed that hikes into a slowing economy because it has to, not because it wants to. When yields fall on a hot print, the market is telling you the growth scare is the bigger story. Watch the 10-year into Friday. If it keeps falling while stocks bounce, the bond market is calling the recovery a relief rally. If yields stabilize, the growth fear is passing.
